unesco.title: Huaconada, ritual dance of Mito
unesco.description: Huaconada is a ritual dance performed in the village of Mito in the province of Concepción in the central Peruvian Andes. Every year, on the first three days of January, masked men known as ''huacones'' perform a choreographed series of dances in the centre of the town. The ''huacones'' represent the former council of elders, and for the duration of Huaconada they become the town’s highest authority. The ''tronador'' (whip) they carry and their masks emphasize this role, the latter characterized by accentuated noses that evoke the beak of the condor, creature that represents the spirit of the sacred mountains. The dance involves two types of ''huacones:'' elders who wear traditional costumes and finely-carved masks inspiring respect and fear; and modern ''huacones'' who wear colourful dress, their masks embodying terror, sadness or mockery. During Huaconada, the modern ''huacones'' dance circumscribed steps around the elders, who have greater freedom to dance improvised movements because of their seniority. An orchestra plays different rhythms, beating out time on a small indigenous drum called a ''tinya.'' Huaconada synthesizes distinctive elements from the Andes and Spain while incorporating new, modern elements. Only those of good conduct and moral integrity may become ''huacones.'' The dance is traditionally passed on from father to son, while clothing and masks are also inherited.

profile.name: Huaconada
profile.tagline: Ritual masked dance of Mito, Peru, performed by elders as village authority in early January.
profile.insight: For three days each January, masked huacones embody the village’s highest authority, wielding whips and condor-beaked masks to dance respect and fear into Mito’s streets.
profile.profile: Huaconada is a ritual dance from Mito, Peru, performed annually on January 1–3 by masked men called huacones who represent the former council of elders. Two types of huacones appear: elders in traditional costumes with fearsome carved masks, and younger dancers in colorful modern dress with expressive masks. The dance is accompanied by the tinya, a small indigenous drum, and features choreographed and improvised movements reflecting moral authority. The tradition is inherited father to son, restricted to men of good conduct.
profile.profile_long:
Huaconada is a ritual dance performed in the village of Mito, located in the province of Concepción in the central Peruvian Andes. Each year, on the first three days of January, men known as huacones take to the village center to perform a series of choreographed dances. These huacones symbolize the ancient council of elders and assume the highest authority in the village during the festival. The huacones wear distinctive masks with prominent noses shaped like the beak of a condor, a sacred Andean symbol representing the spirit of the mountains. The dance features two categories of huacones: the elders who wear traditional costumes and finely carved masks that inspire respect and fear, and the younger huacones who wear colorful modern costumes and masks that express terror, sadness, or mockery. 

The elder huacones have freedom to improvise steps and dance with greater liberty, while the younger dancers move in limited steps around them. The dance is accompanied by an orchestra led by the rhythm of the tinya, a small indigenous drum. The huacones carry whips called tronadores, symbolizing authority and the "traversal of thunder." The costumes include traditional wool hats or chuco, serge garments, rustic leather sandals called llanques, and the masks are wooden with grotesque features. The dance is a fusion of pre-Hispanic Andean and Spanish elements, embodying moral values and social order. 

The tradition is strictly hereditary, passed from father to son along with the masks and costumes, and only men of good moral conduct are permitted to perform as huacones. The dance is a living symbol of the community's identity and social cohesion, recognized by UNESCO in 2010 as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The Huaconada encapsulates a blend of tradition and modernity, ritual authority, and communal memory, performed with solemnity and respect in the high Andes.

sections.origins_and_history: Huaconada originates from the village of Mito in the province of Concepción, central Peruvian Andes. It is a ritual dance with pre-Hispanic roots fused with Spanish colonial elements, symbolizing moral order and social authority. The dance represents the ancient council of elders who governed the village, now enacted by the huacones during the festival. The tradition is passed down through generations, maintaining continuity of cultural identity.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by masked men called huacones in the village center over three days. Two types of huacones dance: elders in traditional costumes with carved masks dance freely and may improvise steps; younger huacones in colorful modern costumes perform limited, circumscribed movements around the elders. The rhythm is set by the tinya drum. The huacones carry whips called tronadores, which symbolize authority. Technique details such as specific footwork counts are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is led by the tinya, a small indigenous drum that beats out the rhythm for the dance. An orchestra accompanies the huacones, playing different rhythms. The sources do not specify other instruments or detailed musical structure.
sections.costume_and_setting: Elder huacones wear traditional attire including wool hats or chuco, serge garments such as a white cape (blanchet), black pants, white apron, wool socks, and rustic leather sandals called llanques. Their wooden masks have grotesque features with prominent noses shaped like a condor's beak. Younger huacones wear colorful modern costumes and masks expressing emotions like terror or sadness. The dance takes place in the central plaza of Mito village.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Huaconada is performed annually on January 1–3, marking the start of the year. The huacones embody the village’s highest authority during the festival, enforcing moral order. The dance symbolizes the traversal of thunder and the power of the condor spirit, linking the community to Andean cosmology and social values. Only men of good conduct may participate, emphasizing ethical integrity.
sections.notable_figures: The dance is traditionally passed from father to son, but specific notable individuals are not named in the sources.
sections.regional_variants: No regional variants are described; Huaconada is specific to Mito village in the Concepción province.
sections.lineage: Huaconada is a folk dance with roots in Andean pre-Hispanic ritual combined with Spanish colonial influences. It is a hereditary tradition passed down within families in Mito, maintaining continuity of cultural and moral values.

profile.sacred_note: Huaconada is a sacred ritual dance representing ancestral authority and moral order; only men of good conduct may perform, and the masks and costumes are inherited and respected.

episode_brief.title_hook: Huaconada: The Dance of Ancestral Authority in the Andes
episode_brief.logline: Discover how masked huacones in Mito, Peru, embody village power through a three-day ritual dance every January.
beats: Opening shot of Mito village plaza at dawn on January 1
Close-up of elder huacones donning carved condor-beak masks and traditional costumes
Younger huacones preparing colorful modern masks and costumes
The tinya drum begins to beat; huacones assemble in formation
Elders perform improvised authoritative dance steps with whips
Younger huacones dance circumscribed steps around elders
Community members watch with respect; explanation of moral and social significance
Closing scene of masks and costumes being carefully stored, passed to next generation
